title: "Design Lab: Notification Delivery and Preferences"

# Design Lab: Notification Delivery and Preferences

Build a Go notification API with email and push adapters backed by fakes. A successful enqueue response promises durable acceptance, while a separate status endpoint reports delivery attempts. Do not equate “provider accepted” with “user received”.

## Model one logical notification

`POST /notifications` takes recipient, template version, channel, variables, and a caller-supplied idempotency key. Authenticate the caller and scope that key to its tenant. Store the payload hash; reuse of a key with different content returns a conflict.

Use three tables: notification intent, channel delivery state, and delivery attempt history. A unique `(notification_id, channel)` prevents accidental duplication when workers retry. Write intent and an outbox row in one transaction, using the [transactional outbox](../../18-distributed-infra/157-outbox-reliable-side-effects.qmd) pattern.

The Go boundary is an adapter, not a provider SDK leaked into every handler:

```go
type Envelope struct {
	ID, Recipient, Template string
	Variables               map[string]string
}

type Receipt struct{ ProviderID string }

type Sender interface {
	Send(context.Context, Envelope) (Receipt, error)
}
```

This is an interface sketch; implement a deterministic fake before a real provider adapter. Classify adapter errors into retryable, permanent, and ambiguous outcomes.

## Dispatch pipeline

A dispatcher claims pending outbox entries, schedules delivery jobs, and records progress. Before each external send, recheck current opt-out and channel eligibility according to the notification category. Partition by recipient if ordering matters. A shared provider rate budget must apply across all workers, not independently at each instance.

Use bounded attempts with jitter and a dead-letter state for permanent errors. Save attempt timestamps and provider receipts, but keep recipient addresses and template variables out of metric labels. Attach context deadlines to adapter calls and bound the queue so a provider outage does not consume unlimited memory.

An external send and your database commit are not one transaction. If the provider accepted a send and the worker dies before recording it, the retry can duplicate the notification. Reuse a provider idempotency key when supported; otherwise document the duplicate risk and reconcile receipts. Do not mark the job sent before the call to hide that uncertainty.

## Acceptance drill

Make the fake return success, permanent rejection, timeout before acceptance, and timeout after acceptance. Crash the worker between provider success and checkpoint. Assert one logical intent, bounded retry attempts, preserved attempt history, and documented handling of ambiguous sends. Unsubscribe during a queued delay and verify the send-time policy.

Expose oldest pending age, attempts by outcome, DLQ count, and provider latency. A low queue depth can still conceal one very old notification. Extend this lab into the [email service](13-distributed-email.qmd), where mailbox storage and transport introduce additional states.
